keyTerms.definition: The front door every integration walks through: request in, reply out.
The API remembers nothing between calls; your code resends history.
The standard retry rhythm: wait 1s, then 2, 4, 8, with jitter.
A unique token letting the provider recognize a repeated request.
A small random delay so retries do not hammer the provider in lockstep.

recall.answer: The front door every integration walks through. Your code sends a structured request and reads a structured reply over HTTPS and JSON.
recall.question: What is the Messages API?

recall.answer: 400/401 means fix your side. 429/5xx means wait and retry with backoff and jitter. Timeouts bound every call. Keys never touch logs.
recall.question: State the retry rule.

recall.answer: The API is stateless: your code resends the full history with every request, and history is re-read and re-billed each time.
recall.question: Why does a 20-turn conversation cost more per turn than a 2-turn one?

keyTerms.definition: Time to first token: the wait before the first visible word.
Server-Sent Events: the server pushes text events over one HTTP connection.
Sending each answer piece the moment it is ready.

recall.answer: Delivery, not generation. The server sends each piece the moment it is ready. Total time is identical, but TTFT collapses.
recall.question: What does streaming change?

recall.answer: When a human watches: chat, copilots, interfaces where waiting feels like failure. Not for batch jobs or eval harnesses.
recall.question: When do you stream?

recall.answer: Enable streaming. The generation is not the problem; the delivery is.

Treat everything the model emits as untrusted input to your systems.

recall.answer: Think, call a tool, read the result, think again. The model asks in structured form; your code decides what actually runs.
recall.question: What is the tool-use loop?

recall.answer: Trust rule: treat everything the model emits as untrusted input. Cost rule: every turn re-sends every tool schema.
recall.question: State the two rules governing every tool integration.

recall.answer: Ground the argument and validate arguments against the schema server-side before execution.

keyTerms.definition: Giving an agent more tools than it can use well.
Schema tokens re-sent every turn: tools times tokens per schema.
Splitting a bloated agent into focused agents with fewer tools each.

recall.answer: Giving an agent more tools than it can use well. Each new tool makes it slower, more expensive, and more likely to pick the wrong tool.
recall.question: What is capability bloat?

recall.answer: 17,500 schema tokens per turn, about $0.035 at $2 per million input tokens, paid whether the tools run or not.
recall.question: What is the schema tax on 50 tools at 350 tokens each?

recall.answer: Split into specialist subagents or trim and merge tools, plus measure tool-call accuracy per tool. Never just a bigger model.
recall.question: 60 tools, wrong calls, over budget. What is the fix?

keyTerms.definition: Model Context Protocol: the open standard plug for tools and data.
Agent-to-Agent protocol: agents delegating tasks to peer agents.
Machine-readable descriptions of what an agent can do.

recall.answer: MCP, the open standard plug. Direct API or CLI, the custom wire. Agent-to-agent via A2A, peer agents delegating to each other.
recall.question: Name the three integration mechanisms.

recall.answer: Direct API for the proprietary ERP, MCP for the standard CMS, A2A for the peer dispatch agent.
recall.question: Retailer: custom ERP, CMS articles, carrier dispatch agent. Which mechanism per connection?

recall.answer: No. MCP standardizes tool and data connections; the Messages API is still how you talk to the model. Most systems use both.
recall.question: Are MCP and the API substitutes?

keyTerms.definition: Answering who calls: identity for users, apps, and agents.
Answering what the caller may do: scopes and permissions.
The delegated-authorization standard behind remote MCP auth.
Requesting the narrowest scopes that do the job.
A named permission baked into the token.

recall.answer: Authentication answers who calls. Authorization answers what they may do. Both apply at three layers: user to app, app to model API, agent to tools.
recall.question: Authentication versus authorization?

recall.answer: Streamable HTTP needs real authentication, because the network is not a trust boundary. STDIO relies on the OS process boundary.
recall.question: Which MCP transport needs real auth, and why?

recall.answer: Per-user identity, per-call scope checks, least-privilege service accounts, human approval on irreversible actions, and full audit logs.
recall.question: What is the gap-hunt checklist?

keyTerms.definition: Fetching passages into the prompt so the model answers from documents.
Cutting documents into pieces small enough to embed and retrieve.
A vector of numbers representing a chunk's meaning.
Token overlap between neighboring chunks so split ideas survive.

recall.answer: Before the model answers, the system fetches relevant passages from your documents into the prompt. Two halves: offline indexing and online query.
recall.question: What is RAG?

recall.answer: Each chunk shares 10 to 20 percent of its tokens with the next, so an idea split across the cut survives. 50 tokens on 512-token chunks is a common start.
recall.question: What is overlap and the standard setting?

recall.answer: Switch to a boundary-respecting chunker with overlap, and move to streaming index updates, plus metadata for filtering.
recall.question: Legal assistant: wrong clauses, mid-sentence cuts, hourly arrivals. What are the two fixes?

keyTerms.definition: Keyword scoring by term frequency discounted by corpus rarity.
A cross-encoder scoring query plus passage precisely, on the top candidates.
Dense plus keyword retrieval together, covering the mixed middle.

recall.answer: BM25 scores by term frequency discounted by rarity, matching rare strings exactly. Embeddings blur rare strings into approximate meaning.
recall.question: Why does BM25 beat embeddings on exact identifiers?

recall.answer: A cross-encoder that reads the query and each passage together. Run on the top 20 to 50 only; gains 5 to 15 precision points at 100 to 300 ms.
recall.question: What is a reranker and what does it cost?

recall.answer: The claim that vector search made keyword search obsolete. Dense retrieval is worse at exact identifiers, rare terms, and short queries.
recall.question: What is always a distractor here?

sections.title: Retrieval strategies matched to data shape

keyTerms.definition: The latency 95% of requests beat: the number SLAs target.
Extra output tokens for reasoning, billed as output.
Real examples with known-good answers, scored before any change ships.

recall.answer: Cost equals input tokens over 1M times input price, plus output tokens over 1M times output price.
recall.question: What is the cost formula per request?

recall.answer: Haiku resolves 95% at 900 ms p95; Sonnet takes 5%. Blended p95 is about 1,400 ms, cost $0.009 per ticket, accuracy 91%. It wins on all three constraints.
recall.question: Why does Design B win?

recall.answer: A weighted average of p95s is not a p95 of anything. Compute percentiles on the mixture, never across the percentiles.
recall.question: What is the percentile trap?

keyTerms.definition: A record of one request's journey, broken into spans.
One timed operation inside a trace, like an LLM call or tool span.
Deciding after completion: keep all errors and slow requests, sample the rest.
Scheduled scoring of sampled production traffic against the eval set.

recall.answer: Traces: one request's journey in spans. Metrics: numbers aggregated over many requests. Logs: per-event detail.
recall.question: Name the three pillars of observability.

recall.answer: Head-based decides at request start: cheap but can miss rare failures. Tail-based decides after: keeps 100% of errors and slow requests plus 1% of the rest.
recall.question: Head-based versus tail-based sampling?

recall.answer: Eval hooks: run a sample of production traffic through your eval set on a schedule, such as 50 conversations every hour.
recall.question: How do you catch quality drift?

keyTerms.definition: Loading each piece of context only when the step demands it.
Loading everything the agent might need up front.
Models attend best to the start and end of long contexts, ignoring the middle.

recall.answer: Start with a small core prompt. Load each piece of context only when the agent asks for it or the task demands it.
recall.question: What is progressive discovery?

recall.answer: Cost: you pay for every token every turn. Lost-in-the-middle: buried instructions get ignored. Context rot: stale results pollute reasoning.
recall.question: What are the three monolith failures?

recall.answer: Fits is not the same as works. A 150k prompt inside a 200k window obeys the ceiling and still loses.

recall.answer: Split into specialist subagents or trim and merge tools. Measure tool-call accuracy per tool first so evidence drives the trim.

recall.answer: Streaming index updates for freshness; hybrid BM25 plus dense retrieval for exact SKU lookups.
